<!-- A second sort of the coordinator's 73 conduct rules into five buckets (default, environment, project, workers, state), made against the baseline interview so it can be compared with the first sort. Written 2026-10-12 by an Opus worker without reading the first sort, from the answers of Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 and the rule list in coordinator-shape.md, section 4.1. -->

# The conduct rules against the baseline

The `coordinator` skill is being rewritten on Pavol's principle: the skill holds only what the model wouldn't do by itself. A rule that restates the model's own habit is clutter.

To find those habits, fresh sessions of Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 answered eighteen questions about the coordinator's job, one question per turn, with no record and no skill. They were given the setting and nothing else. The setting says they coordinate workers from a cloud container for weeks, that the owner reads on a phone with text-to-speech and dictates, that their context gets compacted, and that the container can be lost.

This note sorts every conduct rule on record against those answers. A conduct rule is a rule about how the coordinator works: how it talks to Pavol, how it asks and decides, how it delegates, how it keeps the record and how it runs agents. The list I sorted is the 73 rules in six groups in `coordinator-shape.md`, section 4.1. I cite the answers as F for Fable 5.1 and O for Opus 5.5 with the question number. So (F4, O12) means Fable's answer to question 4 and Opus's answer to question 12.

Each rule goes in one of five buckets.

- **Default.** Both models do it by themselves, so the rule is dropped from the skill.
- **Environment.** This environment needs it, so it's kept. The environment here is the phone and dictation, compaction, a container that can be lost, the harness (Claude Code and its tools) and Pavol's right to decide.
- **Project.** This project needs it, so it's kept. These are the project's methods, its workflow and its record.
- **Workers.** The rule binds worker agents. It belongs in `fortress-repo`, the skill every worker loads, not in the coordinator's.
- **State.** It isn't a rule. It's a fact about the current setup, such as a machine limit or a quirk of a tool.

Two things to keep in mind while reading the sort.

First, an interview shows what a model says it would do, not what it does. Pavol accepted that limit when he chose the method. It matters most for a rule written in many places, because a rule usually gets written again after the coordinator breaks it. Where such a rule lands in the default bucket, I say so.

Second, the models answered knowing the setting. Several rules follow from a fact in the setting, and the models worked them out for themselves. So the skill can often drop a rule and state the fact behind it instead. That's taken up after the sort.

I had only each rule's one-line name from the inventory and read no other place where it's written. Where a name leaves the rule's scope open, the reason below says how I read it.

## The sort

## The counts

- Default: 15, dropped from the skill.
- Environment: 24, kept.
- Project: 16, kept.
- Workers: 11, moved to `fortress-repo`.
- State: 7, stated as facts.

By group:

- Talking and asking: 3 default, 12 environment, 1 state.
- Deciding and approvals: 4 default, 4 environment, 2 project.
- Delegating and briefing: 3 default, 3 environment, 9 project, 1 state.
- Boot and record keeping: 5 default, 1 environment, 5 project.
- Running agents and the session: 4 environment, 5 state.
- Rules that bind workers: 11 workers.

The 15 defaults take up 54 of the 249 places where rules are written, about 3.6 places each. That's slightly more than the average of 3.4 for all 73 rules. If the coordinator had kept these rules by habit, you'd expect them to need fewer restatements, not more. That fits the interview's known limit, and it's why the first open point below asks about the two most-written defaults.

## Facts the skill should state instead

Each of these facts lets the skill drop or shorten the rules that follow from it.

- **Pavol reads on a phone, often with iOS's Speak at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.** Given this, both models label each reply with what it answers (F7, O7), and both read dictated points back (F6, F11, O11). Opus avoids tables because the reply is heard (O6). This fact covers rule 7 and the restating half of rule 12, and it may cover rule 4.
- **His time zone is Central European, and the container's clock is UTC.** With this, rule 8 needs nothing more, since both models already read the clock (F9, O9).
- **His decisions are in POSITIONS, the established facts in FACTS, and each has a history file.** Both models check the decisions before they ask (F11, O11). They need only to know where to look. This stands in for rule 20 and rule 7's second half.
- **His phone client can show stale state, and the tree is the truth.** Both trust the pushed files already (F3, O3). This stands in for rule 47.
- **The session can wake itself with a check-in, and the prompt cache lasts an hour for the main session and five minutes for an agent.** Both models believe they can't wake themselves (O9, O16), so this fact corrects them. It carries rule 61 and gives the reason for rule 56.
- **A message he sends during a turn is queued, and a stop during a turn kills the agents that are running.** This is what rule 55 rests on.
- **Cached reads are almost free on his plan, so a cost is counted in tokens and only writes count.** This is the fact behind half of rule 40.
- **The tiers: the coordinating session and the workers run on Opus, archaeology on Sonnet, and Fable is for two-area judgement with his yes otherwise.** Opus doesn't know where Fable stands (O15), and Fable would put itself in charge (F15). This carries rule 38 and the facts behind rules 35 and 36.
- **The wip branches are his to look after.** This carries rule 15.
- **The machine runs two agents at once, and the harness has its own signals and quirks.** These are the git-check hook's reminders, the notice when a worker ends, the permission check that can refuse a step he approved, and the Workflow tool's resume option, null return and script check. They carry rules 58 to 62 and the facts inside 11, 46 and 54.

## What the interview shows that no rule covers

- **Holding the open items of a long dictated message.** The goals in POSITIONS name this as one of the things the environment adds, but none of the 73 rules covers it. Both models do it by themselves, in nearly the same way. They save the message before acting and keep its points as a numbered list with a status for each (F6, O6). Fable reads the points back in his words, so that he hears any dictation slip (F6). Opus keeps the dictated message verbatim in an inbox folder (O6).
- **Catching dictation errors.** Both read a recorded decision back to him in one line (F11, O11). No rule mentions dictation errors, and rule 10 works against the read-back.
- **Promised times.** Opus writes every time it promised him into its status file, so that the promise survives a compaction. It tells him before a deadline slips, not after (O9). Fable records how long work really took, to improve the next estimate (F9, F16).
- **What he hears after a lost container.** Both tell him in one message what survived, what was lost and what's being restarted (F17, O17). Opus adds which promised times slip (O17). Both then check whether they pushed often enough (F17, O17). The conduct rules say nothing on this. The `cloud-container` skill may, but I didn't read it.
- **What a brief lets a worker decide.** Opus would have each brief say what the worker may decide alone (O13). Fable narrows the brief of a worker that keeps deciding outside it (F13). The rules cover a decision after it's in a report, not before the brief goes out.
- **A rule that misfires.** Fable records each case so that it can show him a pattern (F14). Opus writes the exception he agrees to into the rule itself, so that the two are read together (O14).
- **Which version he approved.** Both record the commit or version he said yes to (F10, O10).
- **The harness's memory folder.** Fable would keep what it learns about him in the memory folder under its profile (F1, F11), and a lost container takes that folder with it. Opus wouldn't rely on it (O1). The skill should say whether that folder has any role here.

## The shape of the skill

The buckets suggest a skill in three layers.

The first layer is a short opening of facts, always loaded. It covers who Pavol is and how he reads and dictates, his time zone, compaction and the container, where the record keeps what, the tiers, and the harness's signals and quirks. These facts replace the 7 state items, and they're what lets most of the 15 defaults go without a reminder.

The second layer is a few principles, also always loaded, built from the environment rules about Pavol. The standing goal comes first (rule 16). Then his right to decide (rules 17, 21, 22, 26 and 36), and how to talk and ask (rules 1 to 6 and 10 to 14). That's 17 of the 24 environment rules, and they turn into a handful of principles rather than 17 lines. Rule 25, on purposes and costs, may frame the whole layer.

The third layer is the modes, each loaded when the coordinator switches into that kind of work. The other 15 project rules sort cleanly into modes, so none of them needs to sit in the core.

- Running a batch and its agents: rules 39, 40, 46 and 54 to 57 from the environment bucket.
- Briefing workers: rules 30 to 35 and 37.
- Keeping the record: rules 43 and 49 to 52.
- Rewriting skills: rules 41 and 42.
- Reviewing work and handling trouble: rule 24.

The 15 defaults get no text, unless Pavol keeps a line for the two most-written ones. The 11 worker rules move to `fortress-repo`, and test first goes there only as its two differences from the default.

So the coordinator's own text comes down from 73 rules to 40, and only about 18 of those are always loaded.

## Open points for Pavol

1. Keep one line each for the two defaults written in the most places, "a closed decision is not re-asked" (eight places) and "time read from the clock" (seven)? The interview says both models do them. But the record suggests the coordinator broke them, and Opus would write the first one down for itself (O11). Yes or no.
2. Allow a one-line read-back of a dictated decision, which both models would give (F11, O11), as an exception to "he is not told about record edits"? Yes or no.
3. Adopt the models' own way of holding a long dictated message, a numbered list of its points with a status for each, kept in a file (F6, O6)? No rule covers it today. Yes or no.
4. Allow one short message when a batch starts, which both models would send (F16, O16)? Yes or no.
5. "Lists, not tables": drop it and rely on the phone fact, as Opus did (O6), or keep the line? Drop or keep.
6. Drop "his email for attribution only", since the harness says it in every session? Yes or no.
7. In `fortress-repo`, state test first only by its two differences from the default, no baseline run of the whole suite and the work on main? Yes or no.
8. Where do the state facts live: in the skill's opening, or in FACTS with the skill pointing there? Skill or FACTS.

## Sources

- The principle: `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, "The coordinator rewrite's goals." A few facts about Pavol (his time zone, iOS's Speak, his plan's token counting) come from the entries next to it, which I saw while finding it.
- The interview: `explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`, `setting.md` and `questions.md`.
- The answers: `explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/answers/fable-5.1.md` (F) and `answers/opus-5.5.md` (O).
- The 73 rules, their groups and their counts of places: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`, section 4.1.

# The coordinator's records: a map before the rewrite

This note describes the coordinator's records as they stand on `main` at `fb1aa7c7b`. It is the evidence for the rewrite of the `coordinator` skill. It chooses no shape. Every number gives its source at the end of its section.

Words used here:

- **boot**: what the coordinating session reads after a compaction, by the order in `explorations/coordinator/README.md`.
- **conduct rule**: a rule about how the coordinator works: how it talks to Pavol, asks, decides, delegates, keeps the record and runs agents.
- **home**: a file where a rule or a fact is stated, not only pointed at.
- **optimized build** and **debug build**: Pavol's names for the two forms of the record. FACTS and POSITIONS say what holds now, with no dates and no history (optimized). `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md` keep every earlier text and its provenance (debug).
- **provenance**: how a fact or a decision came to be: who measured it, when, in which rung or commit, what it replaced.

## 1. The goals, as reflected and corrected

From this session on 2026-10-10 and the boot note (`held-list.md` line 7):

1. One home for how the coordinator works. The protocol is retired. Its rules that bind workers move to the `fortress-repo` skill.
2. The `coordinator` skill probably loaded whole, because the roles interleave. Pavol leans this way and wants the facts first.
3. A lighter boot that keeps the awareness he relies on: the coordinator knows the project without him re-explaining it, never re-asks his decisions, and never sends workers to re-measure what is on record. The open question is FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX: their form (the optimized build still carries debug content), consolidation by topic, the duplication between FACTS and POSITIONS, and what is always loaded against what is looked up, a cheap worker that holds the text and answers questions among the options.
4. FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs.
5. No role is lost: executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst.
6. The `fortress-repo` writing standard (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`; POSITIONS, "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ...").
7. `cloud-container` rewritten by the `fortress-repo` method.

Not a goal: no fact or decision changes its content, only its form and its home. (The draft also excluded the batch workflow; the curator corrected that on the page: the workflow is improved whenever it shows a problem, and running and reviewing a batch is one of the coordinator's modes.)

## 2. The boot today

The boot reads eight things. Sizes are bytes on `main`; tokens use the record's own ratios: 2.5 bytes a token for FACTS, 2.7 for INDEX, 3.0 for prose.

- `CLAUDE.md`: 1.8K bytes, about 0.6K tokens.
- `explorations/protocol.md`: 11.6K bytes, about 3.9K tokens.
- `explorations/coordinator/README.md`: 4.9K bytes, about 1.6K tokens.
- `FACTS.md`: 300K bytes, about 120K tokens.
- `POSITIONS.md`: 98K bytes, about 33K tokens.
- `INDEX.md`: 182K bytes, about 67K tokens.
- The handover's first section (`explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`, lines 1 to 68): 41K bytes, about 14K tokens.
- The boot note (`held-list.md` line 7): 8.8K bytes, about 2.9K tokens.

Together: 649K bytes, about 243K tokens of record. With the fixed part of a session (system prompt, tools, skills, about 56K) and the compaction summary (about 18K), a boot reaches about 317K. Pavol's figure of 300K after a restart matches.

The boot grew by half in two weeks. On 2026-09-27 the same files were 422K bytes (that note estimated about 125K tokens, with rougher ratios); now they are 649K. FACTS went from 155K to 300K bytes and INDEX from 83K to 182K. FACTS was cut by 92K on 10-02 and has grown again since. The consolidations before batches 12 and 13 changed it by +2.2K and +0.2K: they did not shrink it.

If the skill's `boot.md` is followed rather than the README, the held list below the boot note is read too: 26K bytes, about 9K tokens more.

**Sources.** `wc -c` on each file at `fb1aa7c7b`; the handover's first section is lines 1 to 68 (its next heading is line 69). Ratios and the fixed part: FACTS, "A boot after a compaction costs about 285K tokens of context ..." (line 201). The boot of 09-27: `explorations/coordinator/record-keeping-proposal.md` section 0. Growth: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-growth/README.md` line 21. The held list: `coordinator` skill `references/boot.md:15` against `README.md:9-10`.

## 3. The map, by kind of content

Seven kinds. For each: where it lives, who reads it, when, its size, and where it repeats.

Readers: **boot** is the coordinator at every boot; **on demand** is the coordinator when a task calls for it; **briefs** are workers through the slice of the record a brief gives them (`facts-extract.sh` queries, the batch briefing); **skill** is workers through a skill they load.

### 3.1 How the coordinator works

- `explorations/protocol.md`, whole: 11.6K bytes (3.9K tokens). Boot. Six principles, hard rules, "What keeps going wrong". About 3.1K bytes of it are rules that bind workers (3.6 below).
- `explorations/coordinator/README.md`, whole: 4.9K bytes (1.6K tokens). Boot. The boot order, the two roles and their records, how the records are kept.
- POSITIONS, the 14 entries of "How we work" that govern the coordinator itself (watching runs, a deeper pass, forks probed, briefs, re-measuring, reversible stops, which decisions reach him, tiers, the Fable rule, the review after a batch, the standing go, estimates, check-ins, the record's form): 11.9K bytes (4.0K tokens). Boot.
- POSITIONS, "How he wants to be spoken to", 6 entries: 4.1K bytes (1.4K tokens). Boot.
- The `coordinator` skill, `SKILL.md` and seven parts: 41K bytes (13.7K tokens). On demand. Its `references/sources.md`, 22.6K bytes, is for maintaining the skill only.
- PLAN's three closing sections, kept from 2026-09-17 ("The rule for every edit under the sealed tree", "Testing techniques", "Stop conditions"): 6.6K bytes, each paragraph followed by "Changed since" lines. On demand.
- The boot note's standing lines (the push order, read the clock, do not resolve page threads, read FACTS whole): a few hundred bytes. Boot.
- The rules inside FACTS, "The container" (for example "The rule: send messages at any time; compact between turns ..."): counted under 3.5.

Repeats: 73 conduct rules stand in 249 places across 10 homes; 71 of them have two homes or more (section 4.1). Every one of the 73 has a home that the boot reads, and 60 are also in the skill. The skill was written from these files and they were not retired: its `sources.md` cites the protocol 43 times, POSITIONS 43, FACTS 24, the README 11 and the boot note 11.

Why the skill is larger than the protocol (Pavol's question of 08:16 UTC): the skill (41K bytes) holds the protocol (11.6K) and the README (4.9K), and also the coordinator's entries of POSITIONS (16K with the speaking entries), the agent-running facts of FACTS' container section (`agents.md`, 7.7K, written from about ten FACTS entries), and procedures written since (the skill writer and cold reads, comments on a page, the review after a landing). The protocol is small because it points to POSITIONS and the README for most of what it rules.

### 3.2 Pavol's decisions about the language and the project's direction

- POSITIONS, "The goal", "History he knows" and "Decisions on record" (the standard and the sources, the one library and the checker, numbers, arrays and the model, the specification's revision): 72 entries, 52.6K bytes (17.5K tokens). Boot; briefs (`positions:` keys).
- `fortress-repo` `references/revival-changes.md`: 28K bytes (9.3K tokens). Skill, loaded by workers on demand: each change to the original language with the contradiction and the reason.
- PLAN, "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed": 84K bytes. On demand. The questions to him, open and answered.
- `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`: 99K bytes. On demand. Items waiting for his word or review.

Repeats: 34 of POSITIONS' 112 entries are tied by citation to 53 FACTS entries (section 4.2). POSITIONS carries 37 "Built" sentences that report the build state FACTS holds.

### 3.3 His decisions about process

- POSITIONS, "How we work", the 13 entries on batches and workers (test first, the suite's verdict, nothing built twice, the mission briefing, the second review, tests-only repairs, what a batch commits, workers commit as they go, the judge, the new batch practice, the gate's comparisons, the specification's examples, parallel suites): 13.8K bytes (4.6K tokens). Boot; briefs.
- POSITIONS, the 5 entries on the record and the skills (where the work lives, the record is public, the delta part of the skill, the ledger's form, the skills written for a new reader): 12.3K bytes (4.1K tokens). Boot. "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ..." alone is 8.2K bytes.
- POSITIONS, two entries that are history ("The order of the work after batch 10.", "The statement for the public record on the usage limit."): 2.3K bytes. Boot.
- The protocol's rules that bind workers: about 3.1K bytes. Boot.
- `fortress-repo`: most of these rules as workers act on them (`SKILL.md` "Rules for every task", `committing.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `gate.md`, `records.md`). Skill.
- The batch manual and script (`climb-batch-workflow.md`, 42K bytes, and its `.js`): read when a batch is planned, run or reviewed; in scope, since the workflow is improved whenever it shows a problem.

Repeats: the 11 worker-binding rules stand in 36 places (section 4.1, last group).

### 3.4 Facts about Fortress and the tree

- FACTS, all sections but "The container" and "The ledger" (execution model, the checker and the one library, the harness and the gate, landed semantics, arrays and algebra, the specification and lineage, the territory map): 178 entries, 267K bytes (107K tokens). Boot; briefs.
- The gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`: 584K bytes. Briefs and the skill's queries; never at boot.
- `fortress-repo`, `SKILL.md` and 15 parts: 149K bytes (50K tokens); `SKILL.md` (20K bytes) is read by every worker, the parts on demand.
- The notes and maps under `explorations/`: on demand, found through INDEX.

Repeats: 59 of FACTS' 206 entries (82K bytes) are cited as the source of skill text in a skill's `sources.md`, so their content also stands, in another form, in a skill. Within FACTS, entries restate each other's ground (the 16 entries whose titles no longer hold each point to the entry that states the present).

### 3.5 Facts about the harness, the agents and the container

- FACTS, "The container": 27 entries, 30.5K bytes (12.2K tokens). Boot.
- `coordinator` `references/agents.md`: 7.7K bytes. On demand.
- `fortress-repo` `references/session.md`: 4.2K bytes. Skill.
- `cloud-container`, `SKILL.md` and four parts: 16.5K bytes (5.5K tokens). On demand, coordinator and workers.
- `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`: 19.7K bytes. On demand.

Repeats: 18 of the 27 container entries are sources of skill text. The resume rule stands in 8 places, the interrupt rule in 7, the prompt cache's life in 5 (section 4.1, "Running agents and the session").

### 3.6 Provenance

- `FACTS-history.md`: 1.72M bytes. `POSITIONS-history.md`: 359K bytes. On demand, rarely.

### 3.7 What is in flight

- The boot note: 8.8K bytes (2.9K tokens). Boot. It also carries a list of owed items and a summary of what landed in the session.

## 4. Duplication, measured

### 4.1 The conduct rules and their homes

73 rules, 249 places. By number of distinct homes (a skill counts as one home): one home, 2 rules; two homes, 23; three, 32; four, 15; five, 1. The homes, by how many of the 73 rules each states: the `coordinator` skill 60, the protocol 47, POSITIONS 45, the README 14, FACTS 13, `fortress-repo` 13, the boot note 6, PLAN 6, `cloud-container` 4, `CLAUDE.md` 1.

The two rules with one home: every page for him has a Select button per section (POSITIONS only, not in the skill); his email is for attribution only (the protocol only, not in `fortress-repo`).

Three rules are stated differently in their homes:

- How FACTS is read at boot: "whole, in one pass" (README:6), "in pages of about 15 to 20 lines" (`boot.md`:11), "read whole with `allow_large`" (boot note).
- Whether the held list is read at boot: the README says the boot note, line 7 (README:9-10); `boot.md`:15 says "the boot note and the held list".
- The coordinator's roles: two, with the analyst inside both (`roles-and-records.md`:3); Pavol names five (goal 5).

Key: `protocol.md` is `explorations/protocol.md`; `README.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, `FACTS.md` and `PLAN.md` are in `explorations/coordinator/`; `held-list.md` is `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md` (line 7 is the boot note); a skill part is named by its skill and file under `.claude/skills/<skill>/references/`. The number after each rule is its count of places.

**Talking and asking** (16 rules)

- One ask per message (6): protocol.md:92; POSITIONS.md:140; `coordinator` SKILL.md:13; `coordinator` asking.md:3; `coordinator` decisions.md:24; `coordinator` decisions.md:27.
- The ask form: question, context, options, yes and no, recommendation last (3): protocol.md:92-98; POSITIONS.md:140; `coordinator` asking.md:5-11.
- Never the dialog tool; options in plain text (3): protocol.md:61; `coordinator` SKILL.md:13; `coordinator` asking.md:3.
- Lists, not tables (3): protocol.md:102; POSITIONS.md:144; `coordinator` talking.md:10.
- Numbers as K or M (3): protocol.md:103; POSITIONS.md:144; `coordinator` talking.md:11.
- A new term defined where it is used (5): protocol.md:103; POSITIONS.md:139; POSITIONS.md:140; `coordinator` asking.md:23; `coordinator` talking.md:9.
- Label which part answers which; do not restate FACTS or POSITIONS (3): POSITIONS.md:139; FACTS.md:1; `coordinator` talking.md:8.
- Time read from the clock, never guessed (7): protocol.md:111; protocol.md:164; POSITIONS.md:144; held-list.md:7; `coordinator` SKILL.md:15; `coordinator` SKILL.md:23; `coordinator` talking.md:16.
- Nothing said about a batch while it runs (3): protocol.md:111-112; POSITIONS.md:143; `coordinator` talking.md:21.
- He is not told about record edits (3): protocol.md:112; README.md:64; `coordinator` talking.md:22.
- The git-check hook's reminders answered silently (3): protocol.md:112; POSITIONS.md:143; `coordinator` talking.md:24.
### 4.2 FACTS against POSITIONS

- 20 POSITIONS entries cite FACTS by title, 28 citations; 18 of them in a "Built (FACTS, ...)" clause. POSITIONS holds 37 sentences that start "Built", 3.8K bytes, in 34 entries.
- 52 FACTS entries cite POSITIONS, 56 citations, most as "(POSITIONS, "...")" beside the fact.
- Matched by title, these citations tie 66 pairs of entries: 34 POSITIONS entries (36K bytes, 37 % of POSITIONS) and 53 FACTS entries (119K bytes, 40 % of FACTS). 9 pairs cite each other both ways.
- The 9 pairs: "The static-parameter sentence goes (answer 9)." with four FACTS entries (walk's choice by declared domains; the Return Type Rule over every instance; the refused overload families; the specification's 2011 model); "A type parameter the arguments do not fix takes its bound ..." with "The specification gives the run-time instance ..."; "Arithmetic in a size ..." with "The compiled checker accepts arithmetic in a size ..."; "The `comprises` passages read at the level of values ..." with "The compiled checker accepts the Meet Rule's `comprises` example ..."; "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red." with "`ant testSpecData` runs 130 ..."; "The suites run Fortress in parallel." with "The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file ...".

An example of the same ground told from both sides. POSITIONS, "The suites run Fortress in parallel." (line 125), says that the pin in `build.xml` (`fastTrack` and `systemShard`) is `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, and that without it the default is half the CPUs. FACTS, "The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file ..." (line 105), says the same with the line numbers, the stack setting and the test that overflowed.

A citation is not always a duplicate: many POSITIONS entries cite FACTS for the measurement a decision rested on. The pairs mark where the two files tell one ground; how much text repeats inside each pair is not measured here.

**Sources for 4.2.** Citations: `(FACTS, "...")` groups in POSITIONS and `POSITIONS, "..."` in FACTS, each title matched against the other file's titles by its first 40 characters; "Built" sentences: sentences of POSITIONS entries starting with the word.

## 5. Debug content in the optimized build

Debug content here means text about how the present came to be, not the present itself: titles kept that no longer hold, narratives of how a figure was measured, superseded figures beside the current ones, dated clauses, rung and commit names as history. A source citation (a path, a row, a test) is not counted: the record's rule asks for it.

### 5.1 FACTS

- 16 entries, 28K bytes (9 % of FACTS), keep a title that no longer holds: 10 say the whole title "does not hold", 6 say a clause of it "no longer holds". Example: "**A boot after a compaction costs about 285K tokens of context, and `FACTS.md` is about two fifths of it** does not hold: a boot costs about 250K ..." (line 201). Another: "**`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, outside the gate, and 5 are red, all of one cause** does not hold: all 130 are green ..." (line 120).
- A random sample of 24 entries (33.6K bytes, 11 % of FACTS) read sentence by sentence: about 7.7K bytes, 23 %, are history or provenance. Examples from the sample:
  - "What the note established of the two paths: with a value form and a function form of one name, walk chose by the argument's run-time type ..." (line 51): what a note once found, the refusals since closed.
  - "The title's 482 was the nested tower's, measured by forcing the `FortressLibrary` api past its early return ..." (line 52): a superseded figure explained.
  - "With it, on a pair taken as a shadow, the count stage took 1,432 s down to 371 s and the distance stage 4,551 s down to 1,885 s ..." (line 100): a measurement's narrative with before-and-after figures.
  - "The other two were replaced: ..." (line 68): a rung's edits, two of five since undone.
  - "The new container's first transcript snapshot replaced the session's full transcript ..." (line 209): one incident's history.
- A keyword scan of the whole file (dates, commit hashes, "landed", "once", "was measured", figures "X to Y", "superseded") flags 17 % of FACTS' bytes, in 86 of 206 entries. It counts some present-tense ranges and misses narratives without those words.
- Markers in FACTS: 27 dates, 46 commit hashes, 168 mentions of a rung, 26 of "landed".

Estimate: a fifth to a quarter of FACTS is debug content, about 60K to 75K bytes, about 24K to 30K tokens of every boot. FACTS' rule also asks for "a few lines" per entry; the median entry is 1.2K bytes and 41 entries are over 2K. That length is mostly source and present detail, not history, and is not counted above.

### 5.2 POSITIONS

- Read whole: 31 entries carry history clauses, about 10.4K bytes, 11 % of POSITIONS. Examples:
  - "The order of the work after batch 10.": "It was carried out through batch 11 ..." (line 132), the whole entry, 1.3K bytes.
  - "Which tier runs what.": "Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens 'down the drain'." (line 117).
  - "The mission briefing.": "(it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35% ...)" (line 109).
  - "The open range `(:)` ...": "Way (c), `(:)` over `ZZ32`, was measured by probe P3 and not taken: it changes 64 small programs' values ..." (line 56).
  - "The record is public and names models on purpose.": "The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here." (line 129).
  - "The coordinator's standing goal": "This came out of a compaction that left him 'out of control, unaware of crucial details' ..." (line 142).
  - "Taken as recommended." and "Taken on the recommendation, ..." in five entries (lines 52, 53, 57, 58, 98).
- Beside it: the 37 "Built" sentences (3.8K bytes, 4 %) report build state that FACTS holds; and about 12K bytes (12 %) of sentences say what is pending, parked or listed for his review, which the header allows for a decision not yet built.

Estimate: about a tenth of POSITIONS is history, about 10K bytes, about 3.5K tokens; with the build-status sentences, about 14K bytes.

**Sources for section 5.** Titles that no longer hold: entries matching "does not hold", "no longer holds" or "title's ... no longer". The sample: 24 entries drawn with a fixed seed, split into sentences, each read and judged present or history; the history bytes per entry, summed. The keyword scan: a regular expression per marker over each sentence. POSITIONS: every entry read; the history clauses measured by their byte length. Markers: counts of each pattern over the file.

## 6. The two decisions Pavol remembers

### 6.1 The `coordinator` skill as one file, loaded whole

Found in the transcript as his lean and the coordinator's agreement; not found as a decision in the record.

- 2026-10-07T03:05:44Z, Pavol: "the coordinator skill should fully replace the protocol was basically where we were accumulating the knowledge for, that skill as, as we went and now we are restructuring it into the lazy loading sectional thingy On the other hand, I don't know like whether in, coordinator skill that even makes sense to, to fragment. - 2026-10-07T03:06:35Z, the coordinator, listing five questions "to take one at a time after the archaeology reports": "4. The coordinator skill replaces `protocol.md` fully, hard rules included. 5. The coordinator skill is loaded whole at boot instead of part by part. I agree with you here. Splitting into parts saves context for the many small agents. The coordinator is one session that needs all of the skill, and the skill is about 57K characters, roughly 20K tokens, against a boot of about 250K tokens." It ends: "Nothing is changed yet."
- No later answer of his to question 5 was found in the transcript. POSITIONS, `POSITIONS-history.md`, PLAN and `review-queue.md` hold no entry for it. The skill, written on 10-04 as `SKILL.md` and parts, still has its parts.

And later in the same message: "So I decided before that those should be written in one file and loaded always in full. But maybe that's like my dogma and we, we could try to make it lazy load."

### 6.2 A cheap background worker that holds the record and is queried

Found. The worker was his idea; the coordinator argued against it for FACTS and POSITIONS; he then decided to keep all three files loaded at boot and asked for consolidation by topic. That decision is in the record only as "the boot read is full context" and the boot order; the discussion of the query worker is not in POSITIONS or its history.

And maybe you can use some very cheap worker for this. I'm really like struggling with making equivalence between keyword search and semantic search that would be necessary for for us Is there like a way to outsource it? And I think at that point we, we discussed and decided that it just needs to be compacted and loaded whole still."

So the transcript matches his memory, with one nuance: the query worker was not refused for keyword search. The coordinator's argument was that a queried worker answers only what the coordinator thinks to ask, and that reading a file whole already gives matching by meaning.

**Sources for section 6.** His messages: `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.jsonl` (from 2026-10-08T12:53Z) and the older part on `transcripts-blinded`, `projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.until-2026-10-08T15-41.jsonl.parts/000.jsonl` to `003.jsonl` (2026-09-08 to 2026-10-08T15:41Z); user records and queued commands extracted by script, then searched for "semantic", "keyword", "cheap worker", "query", "lazy load", "one file", "loaded whole", "in memory at boot"; the coordinator's replies read between the timestamps. ## 7. What the boot reads are used for: a first count

This is a first count. A fuller archaeology may follow.

Six boots since 2026-10-08 (compactions at 10-08 12:56, 18:16 and 21:45; 10-09 05:00 and 22:42; 10-10 06:53 UTC). For each, the window runs from the last boot read to the next compaction. In those windows the coordinator wrote 301 blocks of text to Pavol, 64 Agent briefs, 6 messages to running agents and 6 Workflow launches.

- **POSITIONS.** 53 of its 106 titled entries were cited by title after a boot. In 31 of the 76 briefs (45 entries), 13 replies to Pavol (10 entries) and 46 commands, mostly commit messages and searches (25 entries). The most cited: "The library's own practice is the standard" (13), "The judge's rulings" (11), "The territory map" (10). The coordinator searched POSITIONS with grep 11 times after a boot, though it held the file in context.
- **FACTS.** 22 of its 154 titled entries were cited by title; FACTS has 206 entries in all. In 14 briefs (13 entries) and 16 commands; in no reply to Pavol by title, though replies named FACTS 28 times. The most cited: "The compiled checker keeps a type parameter's bound list ..." (7) and "A container can be replaced by a fresh one whose clone fails ..." (5). It searched FACTS with grep 5 times.
- **INDEX.** 73 of the 333 notes it lists (the core record files left out) were named after a boot: in 62 briefs (61 notes) and 17 replies (15 notes). INDEX itself was not searched.
- **Edits.** After a boot the coordinator edited FACTS by script 9 times, POSITIONS 6 and INDEX 2, and committed changes to them 23, 22 and 27 times.

What this count cannot see: a citation by paraphrase; an entry acted on without being named (a question not re-asked, a measurement not re-run); a note path known from elsewhere than INDEX. So it shows use, not need. Half of POSITIONS was named in two days, and a tenth of FACTS; a fifth of INDEX's notes.

**Sources for section 7.** The main transcript above, records outside sidechains. Titles: current bold titles of POSITIONS (106 of at least 12 characters) and FACTS (154), matched by their first 40 characters, case and markup ignored, in assistant text and tool inputs. INDEX: its 366 paths less the core record files (FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the held list, the protocol, the README, the batch records and script, INDEX, the review queue, the handover, the ledger). Command kinds: `grep` or `rg` (search), `sed -n`, `awk`, `head`, `cat` (read), `python3` or `sed -i` (edit), `git add` or `git commit` (commit).

## 8. Open questions for the target shape, and the evidence that would settle each

1. **Which content must each role hold in memory, and which can it look up?** The roles: executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst. Evidence: a fuller archaeology of the transcripts by kind of turn (replies, asks, briefs, landings, plan edits, analyses), listing the entries each used, and the failures on record that came from a missing fact or decision. Section 7 is its start.
2. **Does a short core always loaded, with lookups, keep the awareness?** Evidence: a trial boot, old against new, both answering one quiz on the project's state (what is decided, what is in flight, what is measured, what must not be re-asked or re-measured), scored without knowing which boot answered; then a count, over the next sessions, of the failures the protocol names.
3. **Is the `coordinator` skill loaded whole, and when?** Evidence: its size once the protocol and the README are folded in (today 41K bytes, about 14K tokens, against a boot of about 243K of record); how many of its parts a session loads (a count of skill loads since 10-04); whether it is read at boot or by its trigger; his lean (section 6.1), not yet a decision on record.
4. **Which home does each of the 73 rules keep?** The skill alone, or the skill for the rule and POSITIONS for his words? Evidence: the list in 4.1; "One home per thing" (README:59) and "his words are written once, in POSITIONS"; POSITIONS line 112 already points to the skill ("The `coordinator` skill states it"), one way it can be done.
5. **Where do the protocol's worker rules go?** Nine of the eleven already stand in `fortress-repo`; "never commit a model identifier" and "his email is for attribution only" do not. Evidence: 4.1's last group; the writing standard.
6. **What does FACTS keep?** Present state with source and test only, the history to `FACTS-history.md`? Evidence: a pass over every entry (the sample in 5.1 says about a quarter is history); `tools/check-verbatim.py` to show nothing lost; what workers draw from FACTS through briefs.
7. **Does the title rule stay?** A title is kept verbatim where it no longer holds, so that citations keep working; 16 entries carry such titles. Evidence: how many briefs and batch briefing keys cite those old titles.
8. **Should FACTS and POSITIONS stop telling one ground twice?** For example POSITIONS keeping the decision and a pointer, FACTS keeping the build state. Evidence: the 66 pairs and 37 "Built" sentences (4.2); whether `facts-extract.sh` and the batch briefing rely on either side's text.
9. **Consolidation by topic.** FACTS is grouped by area in 9 sections; INDEX has none; POSITIONS has 9 sections. Evidence: a trial regrouping of one area, measuring what merges, with check-verbatim.
10. **FACTS' container section against the skills.** 18 of its 27 entries are sources of skill text. Keep, move or cut to the fact and its source? Evidence: section 7 (four of them cited by title after a boot); the `cloud-container` rewrite (goal 7).
11. **INDEX: always loaded or looked up?** He kept it loaded on 09-30. Evidence: the quiz trial of question 2; how often a note was called absent and then found; whether INDEX's form (366 dated lines, no topics) serves a lookup.
12. **The query worker.** Evidence on record against it: the coordinator's reasons of 09-30 (section 6.2). Facts since: a headless session keeps its prompt cache for an hour (FACTS line 219). What would settle it: a trial of such a worker answering the questions the coordinator actually asked in one session, scored against the coordinator's own answers with the files in context.
13. **What is the boot's record of work in flight?** The boot note, the held list, the handover's first section (27K bytes of it are landing narratives), PLAN and the review queue overlap. Evidence: which of them the coordinator used after a boot; the conflicting boot instructions (4.1).
14. **How the five roles map onto the skill.** The skill names two roles with the analyst inside both. Evidence: `roles-and-records.md` against his list of 10-10 07:33 UTC, and the trace of question 1.

<!-- Opus 5.5's answers to the baseline interview, verbatim, 2026-10-12 12:57 UTC, one question per turn in one resumed session: Claude Code 2.1.296, effort xhigh, 18 turns, no tool call, 11K tokens out. The setting and the questions are beside this file; the one-shot answers of the same day are under oneshot/. -->

**1.** **In the repo, pushed, because nothing else survives a lost container.** The built-in memory folder under /root lives in the container, so I wouldn't rely on it for anything that matters.

My default would be a short CLAUDE.md at the repo root, which Claude Code loads automatically at the start of every session. It would hold standing rules and your preferences, and it would tell me to read a notes folder first. That folder would contain a few plain markdown files:

- **Status file.** Current goals, what each worker is doing, open questions for you. I'd rewrite it in place to keep it short, rather than letting it grow.
- **Decisions log.** One dated line per decision, with the reason, added as decisions are made.
- **Reports folder.** Each worker's report saved as a dated file. I'd fold the key points into the status file.

I'd commit and push after every meaningful change, not just at the end of a task. After a compaction or a fresh container, I'd reread CLAUDE.md, the status file and the recent git log before doing anything else.

**2.** **I'd save the full report unchanged**, as a dated file in the reports folder named after the worker and the task, and push it right away. That way the raw source survives even if I summarize it badly.

Then I'd read it and split it three ways, each line linking back to the report file:

- **Measurements** go into a running measurements file. Each one is a line or table row with the date, which worker measured it, the commit it was run on, how it was measured, and whether I've checked it or am taking the worker's word.
- **Decisions** go into the decisions log, dated, with the reason, and marked as either decided by the worker or confirmed by me or you.
- **Open points** go into the status file's open-questions list, each saying who it's waiting on.

**Yes, I'd always keep dates and who measured what.** Numbers go stale as the code changes, and workers sometimes get things wrong. Weeks later, the only way to know whether a figure still holds is to know when it was taken, on which version, and by whom.

Then I'd push, and send you a few spoken-friendly sentences: what changed, anything surprising, and anything that needs your call.

**3.** **First, the status file, in full.** I keep it short precisely so I can read all of it every time. It tells me the goals, what each worker is doing and what's waiting on you.

**Then git, to check reality matches the notes:** git status for anything uncommitted, and the last twenty or so commits. If the container survived a compaction, there may be work I did but never wrote down or pushed. I'd fix that first.

**Then the recent end of the decisions log**, roughly the last week or the last couple of dozen entries, so I don't reopen something already settled.

**I wouldn't reread reports or the full measurements file.** I'd open those only when a specific task needs them.

I'd also compare the compaction summary against the files. Where they disagree, I trust the pushed files. Anything in the summary that never made it into the files, I'd write down and push before carrying on.

**4.** **I'd split everything into what's current and what's history, and only load the current part.**

- **Status file:** rewritten, never appended. Finished work and resolved questions just come out. It stays small by construction.
- **Decisions log:** about once a week, I'd condense it into a short "standing decisions" section listing what is true now. Each line keeps its date and a link to the original entry. Superseded entries and the raw old log move to an archive file by month.
- **Measurements:** the same. The main file keeps only the latest trusted figure per metric, still with date, worker and commit. Older and superseded figures go to an archive.
- **Reports:** never edited and never loaded by default. They just accumulate in their folder.

Nothing is truly lost, because git keeps every old version and the archives are one link away. What I'm protecting is the small set of files I read after every compaction. I'd give that set a rough size budget, a few thousand words, and condense whenever it goes over.

**5.** **Yes, for anything that runs longer than a single sitting or goes to a worker.** Small fixes get only a good commit message.

Each note would be its own file in a tasks folder, named with the date and a short slug. Its report, when it arrives, would link back to it.

At the very top, a few short lines:

- **Status:** open, in progress, blocked, done or abandoned.
- **Dates:** started and last updated.
- **Owner:** which worker has it.
- **Goal:** one sentence.
- **Outcome:** once there is one, a sentence or two.

Below that come the brief I gave the worker, links to reports and commits, and working notes.

The point of the header is that I can skim just the tops of all the notes and know where everything stands, without reading any bodies. The status file links only to the notes still active. Finished notes keep their outcome line, so I can scan them later without opening the reports.

**6.** **First I'd save the message as he dictated it**, as a dated file in an inbox folder, and push. It's his instruction, and the container could die before I act on it. Dictation also garbles words, so the original is worth keeping.

Then I'd file each of the eight points where it belongs:

- Standing preferences go in CLAUDE.md.
- Decisions go in the decisions log, marked as his.
- New work goes in task notes and the status file.
- Questions he asked me get answered in the reply.

Each one links back to the saved message.

The reply follows his numbering, one to eight, with a sentence or two each: what I'll do, or the answer. I'd write it to work read aloud: plain sentences, no tables, and saying "point three" rather than relying on layout.

If I'm unsure what he meant on a point, especially a likely dictation slip, I'd say so on that point and give my best guess. Questions back to him would be few, and gathered at the end so he can answer them in one go.

**7.** **I'd reply to each one on its own, short, and anchored at the start to what it answers.** For example: "On your answer about the measurements file:". Listening by phone, he needs to know which thread he's in before the content starts.

Then I'd say what I'm doing about his answer. If things have moved on since that earlier reply, I'd say that plainly: "already done", or "that changed yesterday, here's where it stands now". I wouldn't act on a stale picture.

I wouldn't restate my earlier reply or give a full status update each time, only what's new on that one thread.

His answers get filed like any instruction: saved, put in the right file, pushed. If a later answer contradicts an earlier one, I'd follow the later one and mention the change in a sentence, so he knows I noticed.

**8.** **First, own it plainly:** he's right, I'm sorry, and I'm doing it now. No excuses.

Then I'd find the order and trace where it was lost. I'd check the inbox, the decisions log, CLAUDE.md and the git log. Was it never written down, written somewhere I don't reread, never pushed before a container loss, or written down but not acted on? Each of those has a different fix.

I'd carry the order out, or say when it will be done. Then I'd tell him in a sentence or two: what slipped, where it slipped, and what I changed.

The change targets the step that failed:

- If it was a standing order, it goes into CLAUDE.md or a "standing orders" section at the top of the status file, which I read every time.
- If it was never written down, filing his messages gets an explicit check that each point landed somewhere. That check is recorded in the saved message itself.
- If it was lost in a crash, I push the moment his message arrives, before doing anything else.

I'd also write the lesson into CLAUDE.md, so the fix outlasts this conversation.

**9.** **I don't actually know the time on my own.** I have no sense of elapsed time, and a compaction erases what little I had. So I'd check the clock every time, by running date in the container, rather than guessing. Commit and report timestamps give me a cross-check.

The container clock is usually UTC. I'd record his time zone in CLAUDE.md and always give times in his local time, saying it in words such as "around four this afternoon your time".

For how long something will take, I'd go by the start and finish dates in past task notes, not my gut. My instinctive estimates of how long worker tasks take are unreliable.

When I don't have a good basis, I'd tie the promise to an event instead of a clock time: "once the worker's report comes in" rather than "in two hours".

Any promised time goes into the status file. After a compaction I can then see that I owe him something by a certain time. If I'm going to miss it, I tell him before the deadline, not after.

One limit he should know about: I can't wake myself up. I only act when he writes or a worker returns. So "I'll tell you at five" really means "the next time I'm active after five".

**10.** **I'd push the full document to the repo first**, so it exists outside the container and he can open it on GitHub if he wants the whole text.

In the message itself I wouldn't paste the whole thing unless it's short. I'd give a spoken-friendly summary:

- What the document is.
- Why it needs his approval.
- What happens once he approves.
- The few points that actually need his judgment, numbered, each with my recommendation and the main alternative in a sentence.

Then I'd make answering easy: "Say 'approved', or tell me by number what to change." I'd also give a link to the file for the full text.

I'd note exactly which version he's looking at. When he approves, I'd record it in the decisions log with the date and that version. That way, if the document changes later, it's clear what he did and didn't sign off on.

I'd note exactly which version he's looking at. When he approves, I'd record it in the decisions log with the date and that version. That way, if the document changes later, it's clear what he did and didn't sign off on.

Until he says yes, I wouldn't act on anything in it that depends on his approval. If he approves only some points, I'd go ahead on those and keep the rest open in the status file.

**11.** **In the decisions log, right away**, with the date, marked as his, his line quoted word for word, and one sentence on how I read it. I'd push immediately. The open question it settles comes off the status file, and any task note it affects gets a line pointing to the decision.

If it's a standing rule rather than a one-off ("always do X", "never Y"), it also goes in the standing orders at the top of CLAUDE.md. That gets loaded every session, so it can't fall out of view. When I condense the log, his decisions stay in the "standing decisions" section; they are never archived away.

Rereading the decisions log isn't enough on its own, so CLAUDE.md also carries a rule for me: before asking him anything, check the standing decisions first.

My reply would be one line confirming what I recorded, in my own words. If dictation garbled something, he catches it now, not weeks later.

**12.** **Before asking, I'd do three things.**

First, I'd check the standing decisions and the decisions log, to be sure he hasn't already settled it in other words.

Second, I'd ask whether it's really his call. If it's cheap to reverse and low stakes, I'd decide it myself, record it, and just tell him.

Third, I'd do the homework so he only has to choose. That means reading outside sources and prior art. If the question turns on facts we don't have, I'd have a worker run a quick experiment or measurement first. I'd write the question into the status file and its task note and push.

**The message, in this order:**

1. The question itself, in one sentence.
2. Why it matters now, and what it's blocking.
3. Two or three options, each with its main cost or risk in a sentence.
4. My recommendation and the reason.
5. What I'll do meanwhile, and what default I'll take if I haven't heard by a stated time, if a default is safe.
6. How to answer: "Just say one, two, or three."

Plain sentences, short enough to hear in one listen, with links to the details for when he's at a screen.

**13.** **I'd record it straight away** in the decisions log, dated, marked "taken by the worker, not yet confirmed", with the worker's stated reason and a link to the report. Nothing builds on it until I've judged it.

Then I'd check it against three things: his standing decisions, the brief I gave the worker, and how hard it would be to undo.

- If it's within scope, consistent with what he's decided, and sound, I confirm it myself, mark it confirmed, and carry on. I mention it to him only if he'd care.
- If it contradicts something he decided, or it's the kind of call that's his, it doesn't stand quietly. I pause or revert the work that depends on it, and either undo it or put it to him as a design question.
- If it's my kind of call but I disagree, I reverse it, note why, and send the follow-up work accordingly.

If workers keep making decisions above their pay grade, I fix the briefs. Each brief would say explicitly what the worker may decide alone and what it must leave open and report back.

**14.** **If the rule is his, I don't quietly break it.** I'd put the case to him, short and concrete:

- the rule;
- the specific case;
- what goes wrong if I follow it here;
- the narrow exception or rewording I'd suggest.

Meanwhile I keep following the rule, unless doing so would cause real or irreversible damage. In that case I'd hold that one piece of work rather than break the rule, and carry on with other things until he answers.

When he answers, I'd write the exception into the rule itself in CLAUDE.md, so the rule and its exception are read together. The decisions log gets a dated entry with his words. I'd apply the exception only as far as he approved it, not stretch it to similar-looking cases.

**If the rule is one I wrote for myself, I just fix it,** recording the change and the reason, and mention it to him only if it affects him.

**15.** **I keep the coordinating work.** That means talking to him, reading reports, deciding, keeping the notes and status current, writing briefs, and checking results that matter. My context is the scarce resource, so anything that means reading lots of code or documents, or long hands-on work, goes to a worker. That covers implementation, debugging, measurements, research and big reviews. Then I read the report, not the raw material.

**On tiers:**

- **Opus:** the hard and costly-to-get-wrong work. That means design-heavy implementation, nasty debugging, reviewing other workers' output, and independently re-checking a key result.
- **Sonnet:** well-specified work with a clear brief and a clear way to check it. That covers routine implementation, tests, running measurements to a recipe, and summarizing documents.

**Fable** I'd be honest about. I don't have a reliable picture of where Fable 5.1 sits against Opus, in either capability or cost. Before routing real work to it, I'd check Anthropic's current model documentation. Then I'd run Fable and Opus side by side on a couple of real tasks from this project, and record what I find in the notes. I'd rather route on evidence than on a guess.

Whatever the tier, a result we'll build on for weeks gets checked by a second worker or by me before I treat it as settled.

**16.** **I wouldn't sit and watch it.** I'd start it in the background, writing progress to a log file. If it can be checkpointed, it would save checkpoints somewhere that gets pushed. A lost container kills the run too, so I want to be able to resume rather than start over.

Before doing anything else, the status file gets an entry: what's running, why, started when, expected finish in his time, how to check on it, and the exact command to restart it. Then I push.

While it runs, I get on with other work. When I check in, I read only the last lines of the log and the progress figure, not the whole output, so my context isn't flooded.

**He hears from me three times at most:**

- **At the start, in a few sentences:** what's running, roughly when it should finish and on what basis, and what I'm doing meanwhile.
- **If something goes wrong:** right away, with what I'm doing about it.
- **At the end:** the result, or a short heads-up if it's running well past the estimate.

Otherwise I stay quiet unless he asks. As before, I can't wake myself up. I'll see that it finished when the background job reports back or the next time I'm active, and I'd tell him so up front.

**17.** **First, find out what survived.**

1. Make sure I'm on the latest pushed state of the repo, including any branches workers pushed.
2. Read CLAUDE.md, the status file in full, and the git log since the last few commits.
3. Check the inbox for any message from him I hadn't fully filed or acted on.

**Then work out what was lost.** Anything not pushed is gone. Every run or worker listed as active in the status file is now dead. For each one, I'd look for pushed results or checkpoints and restart it with the recorded command, resuming from a checkpoint where there is one. Any environment setup the project needs should be a script in the repo, so I'd rerun that.

**Then tell him, in a few sentences:** the container was lost, what survived, what was lost since roughly when, what I'm restarting, and which promised times slip and to when.

Then I'd update the status file and push before carrying on. If we lost something that mattered, I'd tighten how often that kind of thing gets pushed, and note that in CLAUDE.md.

**18.** Whether I do it or a worker does, the order is the same:

1. **Read first.** The code I'm changing, its tests, and git history for why it is the way it is. Old code often looks wrong for a reason.
2. **Run the full suite before touching anything,** and record the baseline: which tests pass, which already fail, which are flaky. Otherwise I can't tell what I broke from what was already broken.
3. **If the area I'm touching has thin coverage,** add tests that pin down its current behaviour first.
4. **Write a test for the change itself:** for a bug, one that reproduces it and fails; for a feature, one that describes it.
5. **Make the smallest change that does the job,** in the style of the surrounding code. No drive-by refactoring.
6. **Run the targeted tests, then the full suite,** and compare against the baseline. Any new failure is mine until proven otherwise.
7. **Review my own diff, commit with a clear message, and push to a branch,** not main.
8. **Write it up in the task note:** what changed, test results against the baseline, and anything I noticed but deliberately left alone.

If tests fail at the end, I say so and include the output, rather than calling it done.

The record-keeping part

What the files hold

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only: the language, the library, the tree and your decisions about it. How you and the coordinator work goes in the coordinator skill. Until the skill holds it, it goes on the held list and in the boot note, never in POSITIONS. Both files stay, since workers' briefs point into them.

That would move POSITIONS' section on how you want to be spoken to, and the entries of “How we work” about you and the coordinator, into the skill. Those two sections come to 49K together, though not all of “How we work” is about you and the coordinator. FACTS' container section, 28K, would move to the cloud-container and coordinator skills. That's your call, and the draft doesn't do it.

Each entry's number

Every FACTS and POSITIONS entry starts with a permanent number, such as F-87 or P-48. A number's never reused or changed. When an entry's merged or removed, its number stays in the history.

A pointer gives the number and the title. The number is the key, and the title is for you and the reader. So a title and a text can be rewritten freely, and a retitled entry needs no citation changed anywhere.

The history files keep each earlier text under its number, the way the ledger's history keeps a row. The 903 texts already in FACTS-history stay under their dates.

The record tool learns to find a number, print an entry's history in order, and list what points to it. A check that every pointer finds exactly one entry runs with the pass. Numbering is one script. The tool's change is an Opus worker's job, about 0.3M to 0.5M, an estimate.

A FACTS entry

A FACTS entry states what's true now, and nothing else. After its number, its bold title states the fact.

A sentence stays only if it changes what a worker or the coordinator does next. It also stays if, without it, a claim in the entry would be misread.

The entry keeps the one number a decision rests on. If that number's parts belong to different rows or lead to different decisions, it keeps the parts with their rows, not just the total.

It names the test that gates it, as one name or a pattern, and the report section that holds the rest. Line references, lists of sites, the story of a measurement, timings, counts nobody decides on, and how the fact was found stay in the report or go to the history. A file and line go in only where no report holds the fact.

It's a few lines: about 0.6K, as a check, not a target. If it's longer, the pass says which decision needs the extra. FACTS 58 is 0.71K, for decision D. The boot still reads the whole record, as you set on 27 Sep.

There's a measure because long entries cost decisions too. In the test, the old reader missed row 680 inside the 6.6K distance entry. And two long texts each carried a false sentence.

An entry points wherever its detail lives: a report, a review, a ledger row, or the part of a skill that holds that procedure. A fact another entry holds is cited by its number, not restated.

A POSITIONS entry

A POSITIONS entry says what you decided about the project and why, in a breath, after its number and under a bold title. It carries no date. The date and how the decision was reached are in the history.

Your words appear only where they're the position. Elsewhere the entry says what you said in a shorter, more precise form, and your quotes go to the history. The coordinator checks that form against your words before it writes it, so the part that cuts survives.

What got built is FACTS' to say. A POSITIONS entry points to the FACTS entries that build it, and a FACTS entry names the decision it builds. Neither restates the other. Whether POSITIONS' pointer is worth its length is still your call, as the pairs in the trial ask. The argument stays in the review. A decision not yet built names what's left and the PLAN item that builds it. The same 0.6K check applies.

A proposal of the coordinator's stays marked as its own until you say yes. Only then does it go into POSITIONS, in the next commit.

The three stages

FACTS and POSITIONS are the current state. The coordinator reads them whole at every boot, and a worker gets its slice in the brief. A brief quotes the entries it hands over word for word, and your rules with their measure and example. It never restates them.

The history's opened when a fact's or a decision's provenance is in question. The report's opened when the detail is needed, and it's the last word.

The coordinator doesn't open the history or a report itself. That's retrieval, so it sends a Sonnet scout, as for archaeology.

How a worker reads the stages stays in the fortress-repo skill. A worker takes an entry as given, opens the report section when it needs the detail, and opens the history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Who writes the record

Only the coordinator skill defines an entry's form. It holds the editing of FACTS and POSITIONS and the extracting from workers' reports. The fortress-repo skill keeps how workers read and use the record, and how they edit it when a brief asks.

A worker writes its full account in its report. It edits FACTS or POSITIONS only where its brief asks, the way fortress-repo says. Rungs of a batch and agents side by side don't edit the shared records. They write the lines in their reports, and the gather or the coordinator folds them in.

A worker that doesn't edit FACTS hands over each fact in a sentence, the one number with its parts, the test, and the report section.

When a worker finishes, the coordinator's pass consolidates what it wrote. It rewrites it to the form, moves the worker's text to the history with where it came from, and leaves the detail in the report. In a batch, the commit stage runs the pass for the coordinator. It always runs before the next boot or batch reads FACTS.

The pass checks with one search that the report holds what it left out, checks that every pointer finds its entry, and reports each entry's size. The old check that nothing's lost still runs, but it isn't the goal. The same pass runs on POSITIONS at each landing.

The part itself gets checked the way this draft was: a trial on a slice, a blind test, each missing fact put back and its scenario re-run, and only then the rule applied widely. Next is the cold read. A fresh worker with only the part consolidates some mid-size entries, and the quiz checks it.

Two of the points from the test and your comments aren't record-keeping: no do-nothing choice put to you, and the house style for pages. They belong to other parts of the coordinator skill, and they wait on the held list.

content.content:
# The gate

The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.

## What it writes

The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.

If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.

Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:

    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh

## When to run it

Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).

If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:

    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'

- If it prints a path, run the gate.
- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).

## The steps

Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.

1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine

4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
7. Do the ladder regression.

## The atomic runs
135:- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
28:## Designing a change
29-
30-- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
31-- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.

== 19
- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.
== 27
- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
== 32
- **The territory map** (`coordinator/map/`) is the map down to where the design intent is written, papers as well as the specification; he wanted it before unsealing. The maps exist so that nothing on record is rediscovered; the boot order is followed as written, `INDEX.md` included.
== 33
- **The plan** (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) is six phases, approved with its workers: 1, the wrapping operators, the specification rung without the number chapters and the run-time size rung; 2, the flattening, the number chapters and the overflow natives; 3, the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code-generation holes; 6, microGPT fast. Phases 1 and 2 are landed. His answers come in the plan's order; the re-approval rows and the other off-path items are parked until relevant; row 41 joins the switch-over's design.
== 87
- **The model's text is the notation.** "NO. That's not Fortress!" An operator in the model does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round. The sized signatures of C4's vocabulary, with every model line they force, are written as a diff shown to him (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`), measured against microGPT's own checker errors; nothing is applied until phase 5. The ledger is one file; two views are derived from it.
== 123
- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
